KEY MESSAGE 1...A frontal boundary south of the region will 
keep rain chances around through mid-week, especially across 
southern portions of the area.

The cold front that crossed through our region Sunday Night is
expected to stall to our south today, and remain there through
Tuesday. It continues to look like it will lift a little closer
to our region Monday Night into Tuesday morning as a warm 
front, but remain just south of the area. Due to the closer
proximity, and a mid level short wave trough, mean that that
period will have the highest chance for rain across our region.
Given that our low will be on the cool side of the front,
showers are going to be the main mode of any precipitation.
However, isolated, embedded thunderstorms will be possible over
Delmarva, particularly during the day on Tuesday.

For Wednesday into Thursday, the front should again be on the 
move southward, lessening rain chances across the area. 

Confidence is high that temperatures will be below normal
starting Tuesday. In fact, temperatures will likely struggle to
get out of the 60s areawide through most of this week. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...A closed mid-level low ejecting from the Ohio 
Valley is expected to lead to the development of a surface low 
off the Eastern Seaboard during the middle and latter parts of 
this week. Depending on the track of the low, it could bring 
increased rainfall chances to the region. 

Most of the models came into better agreement on the track and
the evolution of the coastal low through Thursday. Through this
time, the center of the low should stay far enough off shore
that rain chances across our region will be very low, except at
immediate coastal areas. However, it looks to be a deep and
intense low, so expect a large pressure gradient, even for
inland areas, and thus breezy to windy conditions. For coastal
areas, we could get close to wind advisory thresholds,
particularly later in the day on Wednesday through Thursday.

Friday into the weekend, some models have this becoming a cutoff
low and retrograding eastward. Notably though, this solution is
primarily with the deterministic, physical equation models.
Several ensemble members and some of the main AI models depict 
this low continuing northeastward. All that being said, the 
forecast, particularly the rain and wind forecast, is very 
uncertain from Friday onward.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Multiple rounds of potentially significant tidal 
flooding expected for this week. The first batch of Coastal Flood 
headlines have been issued with more likely to come. 

With a slow moving coastal storm increasingly likely, the threat for 
tidal flooding has increased. Strong onshore flow that is projected 
to last for several days will result in water piling up across tidal 
tributaries and within back bays of coastal communities. Tidal 
levels will also be enhanced with astronomical tides increasing with 
the upcoming Full Moon on Saturday. This combination of factors will 
lead to widespread tidal flooding, some of which could get to the 
Moderate stage. While not currently forecast, the threat for major 
flooding is not off the table, especially getting near the full 
moon. 

Minor tidal flooding begins as early as tomorrow afternoon and 
evening for some locations. A Coastal Flood Advisory was issued for 
Ocean, Atlantic, and Cape May County in New Jersey and Kent and 
Sussex County in Delaware. For those same areas, tide levels are 
expected to increase for Wednesday and Thursday, potentially getting 
to Moderate stage. A Coastal Flood Watch was issued for Wednesday 
and Thursday evening's high tide. Moderate tidal flooding could even 
continue into the weekend. As mentioned above, cannot rule out tide 
levels reaching major, given the setup. 

For the rest of the NJ coast north of Barnegat Inlet, tide levels 
are currently forecast to reach Minor on Wednesday and Thursday. 
Coastal Flood Advisories likely will be needed, but tide levels are 
currently forecast to stay below Moderate at this time and lower 
water levels than in areas in southern Delaware and South Jersey. 
The same goes for the New Jersey side of Delaware Bay and tidal 
Delaware River. 

Widespread minor tidal flooding is not currently expected within the 
Chesapeake Bay. Usually, strong northeast winds do not result in 
tidal flooding in these areas. 

In addition to coastal flooding, several days of onshore flow and 
high waves will likely result in beach erosion at the Jersey Shore 
and Delaware Beaches.
